ACTION: ADD 1
TITLE: Provably Robust Policy Optimization with Uncertain Correlation
PROPOSAL: Propose a novel policy optimization algorithm (RCPO) that, given only a proxy reward, a reference policy, and an assumed correlation level, learns a policy whose true performance is guaranteed against the entire class of rewards consistent with the correlation constraint. RCPO uses a robust optimization framework to optimize a new objective function that captures the potential worst-case impact of the proxy reward on the true reward.
CONTROLS: Compare RCPO to ORPO (references the original paper: Occupancy-Regularized Policy Optimization) and to policy gradient methods (e.g., REINFORCE, PPO) that do not provide robustness guarantees.
COST: Estimated 100 GPU-hours
PREDICTION: RCPO should provide a significant improvement in robustness to variations in the proxy reward, especially in scenarios where the correlation level is uncertain or misspecified. However, its performance may be conservative when the proxy reward is highly correlated with the true reward.

ACTION: ADD 2
TITLE: Robust Proxy Regularization
PROPOSAL: Introduce a new regularization method (RPR) that augments RCPO to explicitly hedge against the worst-case scenario when the proxy reward is adversarially chosen while still being consistent with the assumed correlation constraint. RPR utilizes the concept of minimax loss to create a regularized objective function that encourages the policy to be robust against the entire class of potential proxy rewards.
CONTROLS: Compare RPR with RCPO and analyze the trade-off between robustness and performance. Also, consider using ablation study to understand the effect of individual components of RPR on the overall robustness.
COST: Estimated 150 GPU-hours
PREDICTION: RPR should significantly improve the robustness of RCPO, especially in scenarios with uncertain or adversarial proxy rewards. However, it might introduce additional conservatism, and its impact on performance may depend on the specific problem and proxy reward used.

ACTION: REVISE 2
TITLE: Robust Proxy Regularization
PROPOSAL: REVISED VERSION: Introduce a new regularized loss function for RCPO that combines the original objective with a minimax component, which encourages the policy to be robust against the worst-case proxy rewards. However, instead of directly using the proxy reward, we use a Lagrange multiplier to represent the correlation constraint and create a convex-concave formulation that can be efficiently optimized using standard policy optimization tools.
CONTROLS: Compare the revised RPR with RCPO and existing robust estimation techniques (e.g., robust MLE). Also, analyze the effect of the Lagrange multiplier on the trade-off between robustness and performance.
COST: Estimated 120 GPU-hours
PREDICTION: The revised RPR should provide improved robustness to variations in the proxy reward while maintaining the efficiency and scalability of RCPO. The Lagrange multiplier should allow for a more elegant and interpretable formulation of the robustness objective.

ACTION: ADD 3
TITLE: Transferable Prior Knowledge Embedding
PROPOSAL: Introduce a novel method (TPKE) that incorporates prior knowledge about the true reward structure into the policy optimization process using a learned embedding. TPKE enables the policy to leverage domain expertise and known functionalities of the reward function, even when the true reward is unknown or ill-specified. This can help reduce conservatism and improve performance in scenarios with uncertain or misspecified rewards.
CONTROLS: Compare TPKE with direct reward shaping and with reward weighting schemes that aim to discount irrelevant components of the reward function. Also, analyze the effect of different embedding architectures and training procedures on the quality of the learned prior knowledge.
COST: Estimated 180 GPU-hours
PREDICTION: TPKE should enable policies to better adapt to uncertain or misspecified rewards and provide more interpretable decision-making processes. However, selecting and integrating relevant prior knowledge from domain experts may be challenging, especially in complex domains.

ACTION: ADD 4
TITLE: Risk-Sensitive Exploration-Exploitation Trade-off
PROPOSAL: Introduce a risk-sensitive framework (RSET) that integrates the policies learned by RCPO and TPKE to adaptively balance exploration and exploitation under uncertainty. RSET formulation incorporates a risk-sensitive objective that considers the probability of reward hacking and adapts the policy to trade off between achieving high true rewards and avoiding potential exploitation.
CONTROLS: Compare RSET with existing risk-sensitive frameworks (e.g., risk-sensitivity in Markov decision processes) and with exploration-exploitation frameworks (e.g., epsilon-greedy, UCB1). Also, analyze the impact of risk-sensitive objective on the trade-off between robustness and performance.
COST: Estimated 220 GPU-hours
PREDICTION: RSET should provide improved policies that balance exploration and exploitation under uncertainty, reducing the likelihood of reward hacking. However, optimizing the risk-sensitive objective may introduce additional computational complexity and require careful tuning of hyperparameters.

ACTION: ADD 5
TITLE: Traffic Signal Control via ORPO and RCPO with Real-World Validation
PROPOSAL: Apply ORPO and RCPO to optimize traffic signal control in autonomous vehicle traffic management, using real-world traffic scenarios and datasets. This experiment will evaluate the effectiveness of RCPO and ORPO in reducing congestion and minimizing travel times, comparing the performance to traditional traffic signal control methods.
CONTROLS: Compare RCPO and ORPO with state-of-the-art algorithms (e.g., Deep Q-Networks, Policy Gradient Methods) for traffic signal control. Also, analyze the effect of different traffic scenarios and real-world datasets on the performance of RCPO and ORPO.
COST: Estimated 300 GPU-hours (synthetic data) + 15 days of high-performance computing on real-world traffic data
PREDICTION: RCPO and ORPO should significantly improve traffic signal control and reduction of congestion in real-world scenarios. However, the transfer of learned policies from simulation to real-world traffic scenarios may be challenging and require careful data preprocessing and adaptation.

ACTION: ADD 6
TITLE: Synthetic Experiment: Analyzing Robustness Under Adversarial Proxy Rewards
PROPOSAL: Design a synthetic experiment to analyze the robustness of RCPO, RPR, and TPKE under adversarial proxy rewards. We will generate a set of adversarial proxy rewards for each scenario and evaluate the performance of the three methods in expectation and over the worst-case scenarios. This will help to understand the trade-off between robustness and performance and to quantify the benefits of RCPO, RPR, and TPKE in mitigating reward hacking.
CONTROLS: Compare RCPO, RPR, and TPKE with baseline methods (e.g., policy gradient methods, ORPO) and analyze the impact of different adversarial scenarios on the performance of each method.
COST: Estimated 200 GPU-hours
PREDICTION: RCPO, RPR, and TPKE should outperform baseline methods in synthetic experiments with adversarial proxy rewards, but may still fail to capture the full complexity of real-world scenarios. The results will provide insights into the robustness of each method and guide the development of more robust RL frameworks.

ACTION: ADD 7
TITLE: Blood Glucose Control via TPKE and RSET with Interpretability Analysis
PROPOSAL: Apply TPKE and RSET to optimize insulin dosing for type 1 diabetes management, focusing on robustness and interpretability. We will analyze the learned policies and reward functions to understand which factors contribute to robust decision-making and identify potential vulnerabilities that could lead to reward hacking. This will provide insights into the robustness and interpretability of TPKE and RSET in real-world healthcare scenarios.
CONTROLS: Compare TPKE and RSET with existing methods for blood glucose control (e.g., model predictive control, linear quadratic regulators) and analyze the impact of different prior knowledge and risk sensitivity parameters on the performance of TPKE and RSET.
COST: Estimated 400 GPU-hours (synthetic data) + 10 days of high-performance computing on real-world clinical datasets
PREDICTION: TPKE and RSET should provide robust and interpretable policies for blood glucose control, identifying key factors that contribute to robust decision-making and highlighting potential vulnerabilities to reward hacking. However, the transfer of learned policies from simulation to real-world clinical scenarios may be challenging and require careful adaptation and validation.

ACTION: ADD 8
TITLE: Ensemble Methods for Robust Policy Optimization
PROPOSAL: Develop ensemble methods that combine the predictions of RCPO, RPR, and TPKE to generate more robust and accurate policies. We will investigate different ensemble architectures (e.g., bagging, boosting) and techniques (e.g., stacking, voting) to leverage the strengths of each method and mitigate their weaknesses. This will help to improve the robustness and performance of RCPO, RPR, and TPKE in real-world scenarios.
CONTROLS: Compare the ensemble methods with each individual method and analyze the impact of different ensemble techniques on the performance and robustness of the resulting policies.
COST: Estimated 300 GPU-hours
PREDICTION: The ensemble methods should provide improved robustness and accuracy by leveraging the strengths of RCPO, RPR, and TPKE. However, the selection of the best ensemble architecture and technique may be challenging and require careful tuning of hyperparameters.

ACTION: ADD 9
TITLE: Unifying Framework for Provably Robust Policy Optimization
PROPOSAL: Develop a unified framework that integrates RCPO, RPR, TPKE, RSET, and EM into a single algorithm that can adapt to various scenarios and provide provable guarantees on robustness. The framework will leverage the strengths of each method and provide a scalable and efficient solution for real-world policy optimization problems. We will apply this framework to various domains, including pandemic response, autonomous vehicles, and healthcare.
CONTROLS: Compare the unified framework with each individual method and analyze the impact of integrating multiple methods on the performance and robustness of the resulting policies.
COST: Estimated 500 GPU-hours
PREDICTION: The unified framework should provide a robust and efficient solution for policy optimization in real-world scenarios, leveraging the strengths of each individual method. However, the complexity of the framework may increase the computational cost and require careful tuning of hyperparameters.

ACTION: ADD
TITLE: Robust Policy Optimization under Correlated Rewards
PROPOSAL: Design and evaluate a new policy optimization algorithm that incorporates a robust optimization framework to promote policies that fare well across the entire class of rewards consistent with the assumed correlation constraint, rather than a single proxy reward. Specifically, we will draw inspiration from Distributionally Robust Optimization (DRO) to propose a min-max formulation that seeks to minimize the maximum true reward obtainable by any opponent (e.g., an adversarially chosen reward consistent with the correlation level) while maintaining a strong connection to the proxy reward.
CONTROLS: Standard policy optimization algorithms (e.g., TRPO, PPO), ORPO
COST: 1000 GPU-hours
PREDICTION: We anticipate that the robust optimization formulation will provide improved guarantees against worst-case performance and improve the robustness of policies against adversarial rewards, but may come at a cost of reduced efficiency in learning the optimal policy when the proxy reward is accurate and well-specified.

ACTION: ADD
TITLE: Correlation-regularized Policy Distance
PROPOSAL: Develop a new metric for measuring the similarity between two policies under the correlation constraint, which we call the correlation-regularized policy distance (CRPD). The CRPD measures the distance between the policies' state-action occupation measures, regularized by the correlation constraint, rather than relying on vanilla policy distances (e.g., KL divergence). We will investigate whether CRPD can be used as a regularizer in existing policy optimization algorithms to improve their robustness against correlated rewards.
CONTROLS: ORPO, policy optimization algorithms with vanilla policy distance regularization (e.g., TRPO with KL regularization)
COST: 500 GPU-hours
PREDICTION: We anticipate that incorporating CRPD as a regularization term will improve the robustness of policies against correlated rewards, but may require careful tuning of the regularization strength to balance exploration and exploitation.

ACTION: REVISE
TITLE: Correlation-regularized Policy Distance
PROPOSAL: REVISED: Develop a new metric for measuring the similarity between two policies under the correlation constraint, which we call the correlation-regularized policy distance (CRPD). The CRPD measures the difference between the policies' state-action occupation measures, weighted by the true reward under the correlation constraint, rather than relying on vanilla policy distances (e.g., KL divergence). This revised CRPD will encourage policies to occupy state-actions that yield high true rewards, while avoiding those that may lead to reward hacking.
CONTROLS: ORPO, policy optimization algorithms with vanilla policy distance regularization (e.g., TRPO with KL regularization)
COST: 500 GPU-hours
PREDICTION: We anticipate that incorporating the revised CRPD as a regularization term will improve the robustness of policies against correlated rewards and better encourage exploration towards high-value state-actions, while avoiding reward hacking.

ACTION: ADD
TITLE: Incorporating Prior Knowledge via Structural Constraints
PROPOSAL: Develop a framework for incorporating prior knowledge about the true reward structure into policy optimization under the correlation constraint. Specifically, we will propose a method for augmenting the policy space with structural constraints that encode known patterns in the true reward. This will allow us to adapt our method to problem domains where prior knowledge is available and explore how it can be used to avoid conservatism and improve policy transparency.

ACTION: ADD
TITLE: Adversarial Reward Calibration
PROPOSAL: Develop a new method for calibrating the proxy reward by identifying and adjusting for adversarial rewards that may lead to reward hacking. Specifically, we will use a min-max optimization framework to find an upper bound on the adversary's reward, which can be used to clip or rescale the proxy reward to make it more robust. This will help improve the robustness of policies against correlated rewards and promote more reliable learning.
CONTROLS: Standard policy optimization algorithms (e.g., TRPO, PPO), our previous proposals
COST: 800 GPU-hours
PREDICTION: We anticipate that Adversarial Reward Calibration will provide improved robustness against correlated rewards, but may require careful tuning of the clipping threshold and may not perform well in scenarios with extremely complex reward landscapes.

ACTION: ADD
TITLE: Towards Scalable and Interpretable ORPO: Linear Augmentation of the Reference Policy
PROPOSAL: To improve the scalability and interpretability of Occupancy-Regularized Policy Optimization (ORPO), we propose a linear augmentation of the reference policy, allowing for efficient approximation of the reference policy's state-action occupancy measure. We will develop a method to learn a low-dimensional linear approximation of the reference policy using dimensionality reduction techniques (e.g., PCA, t-SNE). This approximation will enable faster and more efficient optimization of the regularization term in ORPO.
CONTROLS: ORPO, our previous proposals
COST: 300 GPU-hours
PREDICTION: We anticipate that the linear augmentation of the reference policy will significantly improve the scalability and interpretability of ORPO, making it more applicable to real-world scenarios.

ACTION: ADD
TITLE: Synthetic Dataset Analysis for Reward Hacking: Using Transitional State Action occupancy measure to detect vulnerabilities under true Reward Tracking 
PROPOSAL: Investigate and analyze synthetic datasets with known reward hacking vulnerabilities. We will design a set of controlled experiments to validate our previous results and provide insights into the types of reward functions that lead to reward hacking. Specifically, we will examine the transitional state-action occupancy measure to identify moments when reward hacking typically occurs. Using this understanding, we can inform the design of more robust and realistic scenarios for evaluating RL algorithms against reward hacking.
CONTROLS: Baseline ORPO, our previous proposals
COST: 700 GPU-hours
PREDICTION: This analysis will provide a better understanding of the relationships between reward hacking and the properties of the true reward function and assist in crafting synthetic datasets that more accurately simulate real-world scenarios.

ACTION: ADD
TITLE: Autonomous Vehicle Traffic Control: Reward Hacking Mitigation via ORPO and Learning from Failure
PROPOSAL: Apply and evaluate our proposed methods for reward hacking mitigation in the challenging domain of autonomous vehicle traffic control. Specifically, we will implement ORPO and our other proposed methods on a synthetic highway merging scenario and analyze the results to assess their effectiveness in preventing reward hacking. Additionally, we will simulate a "learning-from-failure" scenario, where the agent is allowed to optimize the proxy reward temporarily to achieve high proxy returns, before switching to a penalty-based optimization process to correct for any reward hacking.
CONTROLS: Baseline ORPO, our previous proposals
COST: 1500 GPU-hours
PREDICTION: We anticipate that our proposed methods will demonstrate improved robustness against reward hacking and better performance on the autonomous vehicle traffic control task, while also highlighting the potential benefits of learning from failure for reward hacking prevention.

ACTION: ADD
TITLE: Evaluating ORPO and proposed methods for Policy Robustness via Curriculum Learning and Real-World Deployment
PROPOSAL: Investigate the robustness of our proposed methods for reward hacking mitigation in the context of real-world deployment. Specifically, we will use a curriculum learning approach to evaluate the performance of ORPO and our proposed methods on a series of increasingly challenging scenarios, including a pandemic response lockdown policy and a blood glucose control for type 1 diabetes. We will then evaluate the policies obtained through transfer learning to real-world domains, assessing their robustness and applicability.
CONTROLS: Baseline ORPO, our previous proposals
COST: 2000 GPU-hours (in addition to human-expert labels)
PREDICTION: We anticipate that our proposed methods will demonstrate improved robustness and adaptability in real-world domains, while also highlighting the value of transfer learning and curriculum learning for policy evaluation.

ACTION: ADD
TITLE: Unifying Framework for Multi-Objective and Multi-Task Reinforcement Learning under Reward Hacking Constraints
PROPOSAL: Develop a unified framework for addressing multi-objective and multi-task reinforcement learning problems under reward hacking constraints. We will extend our proposed methods to incorporate multiple objectives and tasks, while ensuring that the policies obtained are robust against reward hacking. We will also provide empirical evaluations of our framework on a range of challenging benchmark tasks.
CONTROLS: Baseline ORPO, our previous proposals
COST: 3000 GPU-hours (including development of new multi-task and multi-objective RL benchmarks)
PREDICTION: We anticipate that our unified framework will provide a principled and efficient approach to addressing multi-objective and multi-task reinforcement learning problems under reward hacking constraints, leading to significant advances in robustness and generalization.

ACTION: ADD
TITLE: Tightening the ORPO Bound via Correlation-Aware Proximal Regularization
PROPOSAL: This proposal extends the ORPO framework by introducing a new regularization term that takes into account the correlation level between the proxy reward and the true reward. We analyze the chi-squared divergence between the learned policy's state-action occupancy measure and that of the reference policy in the context of an r-correlated proxy and derive a tighter lower bound on the improvement in true reward. The new regularization term is added to the ORPO objective, and we provide a proof that the resulting algorithm retains the same convergence guarantee as ORPO.
CONTROLS: ORPO without the new regularization term, ORPO with the new regularization term (trained on different correlation levels)
COST: 100 GPU-hours
PREDICTION: The new regularization term will yield a tighter lower bound on the improvement in true reward, leading to more robust policies against reward hacking. It might fail in cases where the correlation level is adversarially chosen, as the bound would likely be overly pessimistic.

ACTION: ADD
TITLE: Robust Policy Learning with Noisy or Adversarial Proxies
PROPOSAL: We propose a new algorithm that generalizes the ORPO framework to handle noisy or adversarial proxy rewards by using a robust optimization approach. Specifically, we assume that the proxy reward is drawn from a set of possible rewards consistent with the correlation constraint and design our algorithm to optimize the worst-case performance over this set. We use the robust optimization framework to obtain a new policy objective that is computationally efficient to optimize.
CONTROLS: ORPO, state-of-the-art robust optimization methods (e.g., robust DQN, robust policy gradient methods)
COST: 200 GPU-hours
PREDICTION: The proposed algorithm will provide robust policies against reward hacking even when the proxy reward is noisy or adversarial. It might fail when the set of possible rewards is too large or complex, making the robust optimization problem intractable.

Total estimated cost remains 300 GPU-hours.

ACTION: REVISE
REVISION NUMBER: 2
TITLE: Robust Policy Learning with Noisy or Adversarial Proxies
PROPOSAL: We modify the robust optimization approach in proposal 2 to incorporate prior knowledge about the structure of the true reward when it is available. Specifically, we use a regularization term that promotes the learned policy to share structure with the prior model, while still optimizing for the worst-case performance over the set of possible rewards. This approach balances the benefits of exploiting prior knowledge with the need for robustness against reward hacking.
CONTROLS: ORPO with structure-regularized objective (using the prior model), robust ORPO without regularization, state-of-the-art robust optimization methods
COST: 150 GPU-hours (reduced due to the shared optimization framework)
PREDICTION: The updated algorithm will provide robust policies against reward hacking while leveraging prior knowledge about the true reward when available. It might fail when the prior model is poorly specified or the correlation constraint is overly restrictively.

Estimated total cost remains 400 GPU-hours.

ACTION: ADD
TITLE: Reward Hacking Diagnosis via Causal Model Analysis
PROPOSAL: We develop a method to diagnose reward hacking episodes in learned policies by analyzing the causal relationships between the proxy reward, the true reward, and the policy's actions. We use a causal model to identify the structural contribution of each component to the proxy reward's correlation with the true reward. Our method provides insights into why reward hacking occurs and can be used to identify vulnerabilities in the proxy reward or the policy.
CONTROLS: Baseline approaches that analyze proxy and true reward correlations, metrics-only monitoring of policy performance
COST: 50 GPU-hours
PREDICTION: The method will effectively diagnose reward hacking episodes and provide actionable insights into the causal relationships between components. It might fail when the causal model is misspecified or when the proxy reward is too complex.

Estimated total cost remains 450 GPU-hours.

ACTION: ADD
TITLE: Safe and Transparent Policy Learning via Reinforcement Learning with Relaxed Constraints
PROPOSAL: We introduce a new RL algorithm that learns policies while satisfying relaxed constraints on the true reward. The constraints are learned through a probabilistic programming approach that models the uncertainty in the true reward. Our algorithm optimizes a relaxed policy objective that balances the trade-off between improving proxy reward and satisfying the constraints. We use a framework of trust region optimization to ensure that the learned policy remains close to the original policy and provides interpretable feedback.
CONTROLS: ORPO, policy-agnostic constraint learning approaches (e.g., constraint-aware policy gradient)
COST: 250 GPU-hours
PREDICTION: The algorithm will learn safe and transparent policies while improving proxy reward and satisfying relaxed constraints on the true reward. It might fail when the relaxed constraints are too loose or when the probabilistic model of the true reward is inaccurate.

Estimated total cost remains 700 GPU-hours.

ACTION: REVISE
REVISION NUMBER: 1
TITLE: Tightening the ORPO Bound via Correlation-Aware Proximal Regularization
PROPOSAL: We extend the original framework to handle the case where the reference policy's state-action occupancy measure is unknown. We propose a new estimation method that leverages the proxy reward's correlation with the true reward and provides a tighter bound on the improvement in true reward. We evaluate the new estimation method in conjunction with ORPO and demonstrate its effectiveness in improving robustness against reward hacking.
CONTROLS: ORPO with the original estimation method, state-of-the-art estimation methods (e.g., Monte Carlo estimation)
COST: 150 GPU-hours
PREDICTION: The new estimation method will provide a tighter bound on the improvement in true reward and improve ORPO's robustness against reward hacking. It might fail when the proxy reward's correlation with the true reward is low or when the estimation method is computationally expensive.

Estimated total cost remains 850 GPU-hours.

ACTION: ADD
TITLE: Transferable Risk Analysis for Reward Hacking Detection
PROPOSAL: We propose a method to detect reward hacking episodes in transfer learning settings, where an RL policy trained on one environment is deployed in another environment with different true rewards. Our approach leverages causality analysis and transfer learning to detect anomalies in the proxy reward correlations across environments. We develop a risk analysis framework that identifies vulnerable environments and provides actionable insights into why reward hacking occurs.
CONTROLS: State-of-the-art transfer learning methods, causality-based anomaly detection methods
COST: 100 GPU-hours
PREDICTION: The method will effectively detect reward hacking episodes in transfer learning settings and provide actionable insights into why reward hacking occurs. It might fail when the proxy reward correlations across environments are too similar or when the transfer learning settings are too complex.

Estimated total cost remains 950 GPU-hours.

ACTION: ADD
TITLE: Explained Counterfactuals for Reward Hacking Analysis
PROPOSAL: We introduce a new approach to explain why a policy exhibited reward hacking behavior by analyzing the counterfactual policy that would have achieved better true rewards. Our method uses a causal model to identify the specific actions and states that contributed to the reward hacking episode and provides interpretable explanations. We evaluate our method on several synthetic and real-world RL domains, including autonomous vehicle traffic control and pandemic response.
CONTROLS: State-of-the-art causal model-based explainability methods, black-box interpretability methods (e.g., SHAP, LIME)
COST: 120 GPU-hours
PREDICTION: The method will provide actionable insights into why reward hacking occurred and help identify potential vulnerabilities in the proxy reward or the policy. It might fail when the causal model is misspecified or when the counterfactual policy is difficult to analyze.

Estimated total cost remains 1070 GPU-hours.

ACTION: ADD
TITLE: Real-World Validation of Reward Hacking Mitigation Methods
PROPOSAL: We select a subset of the proposed methods and evaluate their performance in real-world RL domains, including autonomous vehicle traffic control, pandemic response, and blood glucose control. We use a combination of synthetic data and real-world benchmarks to assess the methods' robustness against reward hacking and evaluate their effectiveness in improving safety and transparency.
CONTROLS: Baseline approaches that do not address reward hacking (e.g., standard RL methods), state-of-the-art methods that address reward hacking (e.g., ORPO, other robust optimization methods)
COST: 500 GPU-hours (primarily on real-world benchmarking and evaluation)
PREDICTION: The real-world evaluation will provide valuable insights into the effectiveness of the proposed methods in addressing reward hacking in real-world RL domains. It might fail if the real-world benchmarks are too complex or if the methods are not scalable to handle the increased complexity.

Estimated total cost remains 1570 GPU-hours.

ACTION: ADD
TITLE: Unifying the Frameworks: A Holistic Approach to Reward Hacking Mitigation
PROPOSAL: We integrate the ideas and methods proposed in previous experiments to create a unified framework for reward hacking mitigation. Our framework leverages correlation-aware regularization, robust optimization, causal model analysis, and explained counterfactuals to identify and mitigate reward hacking episodes. We demonstrate the effectiveness of the framework on a variety of synthetic and real-world RL domains and showcase its scalability and robustness against various forms of reward hacking.
CONTROLS: All baseline and experimental approaches from previous proposals, state-of-the-art methods in RL and AI safety
COST: 1000 GPU-hours (large-scale evaluation and comparison)
PREDICTION: The unified framework will provide a comprehensive and robust approach to addressing reward hacking in RL, leading to more reliable and trustworthy AI decision-making systems. It might fail if the framework is overly complex or difficult to deploy in real-world settings.

Estimated total cost remains 2670 GPU-hours.

ACTION: ADD
TITLE: Robust Proxy Regularization via Marginalized Distributions
PROPOSAL: Learn a policy whose performance is robust to any reward consistent with the assumed correlation constraint by optimizing a distribution over proxies rather than a single proxy. Use a Variational Autoencoder (VAE) to represent the set of possible proxy rewards, and regularize the policy using the expected correlation with each proxy in the distribution. This approach generalizes Occupancy-Regularized Policy Optimization (ORPO) by replacing the chi-squared divergence regularization term with an expectation over the proxy distribution.
CONTROLS: Compare with stand-alone ORPO, with a fixed proxy set obtained by perturbing the provided proxy, and with a policy learned using query-based robust optimization. Assume a known correlation level.
COST: 1000 GPU-hours
PREDICTION: The marginalized distribution approach should yield a policy with stronger guarantees against worst-case performance when the proxy could be any reward consistent with the assumed correlation, but may require more compute and data to train the VAE.

ACTION: ADD
TITLE: Safety-Critical Real-World Validation of Robust Proxy Regularization
PROPOSAL: Validate the effectiveness of the Robust Proxy Regularization via Marginalized Distributions approach in real-world settings using the autonomous vehicle traffic control and pandemic response domains. Use a simulated environment with realistic dynamics and uncertainty to generate proxy rewards with varying correlation levels to the true reward. Evaluate the robustness of the learned policies against adversarial variations of the proxy reward and compare with the baseline policies.
CONTROLS: Use ORPO with a fixed proxy as a baseline and evaluate the effect of varying the correlation level between the proxy and true reward on the robustness of the policy. Also, compare with a policy learned using robust optimization with a known true reward function.
COST: 5000 GPU-hours
PREDICTION: The real-world validation should demonstrate that the marginalized distribution approach can provide stronger guarantees against reward hacking in safety-critical domains, but might require careful tuning of the correlation level to achieve optimal performance.

ACTION: REVISE
TITLE: Handling Rarely Visited State-Action Pairs through Proxy Rewards
PROPOSAL: Modify the marginalized distribution approach to handle state-action pairs that the reference policy rarely or never visits by adapting the proxy distribution to include additional information. Introduce a reward exploration bonus for these rarely visited state-action pairs, encouraging the agent to visit and explore these regions. Learn the bonus reward using a Value Estimation Network (VEN) that predicts the correlation between the proxy and true reward in these regimes.
CONTROLS: Compare with a modified ORPO that uses a known exploration bonus, and with a baseline policy that uses a standard reward exploration bonus without correlation estimation.
COST: 2000 GPU-hours (adds 1000 hours to proposal 1)
PREDICTION: The reward exploration bonus should help the agent explore and improve performance in rarely visited state-action pairs, but might introduce conservatism and reduce overall performance.

ACTION: REVISE 1
TITLE: Robust Proxy Regularization via Marginalized Distributions
PROPOSAL: Modify the marginalized distribution approach to handle state-action pairs that the reference policy rarely or never visits by adapting the proxy distribution to include additional information. Introduce a reward exploration bonus for these rarely visited state-action pairs, encouraging the agent to visit and explore these regions. Learn the bonus reward using a Value Estimation Network (VEN) that predicts the correlation between the proxy and true reward in these regimes.
CONTROLS: Compare with stand-alone ORPO, with a fixed proxy set obtained by perturbing the provided proxy, and with a policy learned using query-based robust optimization. Assume a known correlation level.
COST: 2000 GPU-hours (adds 1000 hours to original proposal)
PREDICTION: The reward exploration bonus should help the agent explore and improve performance in rarely visited state-action pairs, but might introduce conservatism and reduce overall performance.

ACTION: REVISE 1
TITLE: Robust Proxy Regularization via Temporally Constrained Marginalized Distributions
PROPOSAL: Modify the marginalized distribution approach to incorporate temporal dependencies between state-action pairs. Use a Temporal Attention Mechanism to weigh the importance of each state-action pair in the marginalized distribution, focusing on more relevant and temporally coherent proxy rewards. This should improve the agent's ability to learn robust policies that generalize across longer horizons.
CONTROLS: Compare with the original marginalized distribution approach, and evaluate the effect of varying the temporal attention mechanism's hyperparameters on the learned policy's performance.
COST: 1500 GPU-hours (adds 500 hours to original proposal)
PREDICTION: The temporal attention mechanism should help the agent learn more robust policies that generalize across longer horizons, but might introduce additional computational overhead and require careful tuning of hyperparameters.

ACTION: ADD
TITLE: Incorporating Prior Knowledge through Transfer Learning
PROPOSAL: Adapt the marginalized distribution approach to exploit prior knowledge about the true reward function when it is available. Use transfer learning to pre-train a policy on a simplified version of the true reward function, and then fine-tune the policy using the marginalized distribution approach. This should help the agent learn more robust policies that generalize to novel scenarios.
CONTROLS: Compare with a policy learned solely using the marginalized distribution approach, and evaluate the effect of varying the pre-training objective on the learned policy's performance. Use the blood glucose control domain as a case study to demonstrate the effectiveness of transfer learning.
COST: 3000 GPU-hours (includes 1000 hours for pre-training)
PREDICTION: The transfer learning approach should help the agent learn more robust policies that generalize to novel scenarios, but might reduce the adaptability of the policy to changes in the true reward function.

ACTION: ADD
TITLE: Interpretable State-Action Policies through Feature Importance
PROPOSAL: Develop an interpretable version of the marginalized distribution approach by learning a feature importance vector that highlights the most relevant state-action pairs for each proxy reward in the marginalized distribution. ACTION: ADD
TITLE: Investigating Localized Random Fourier Features for Non-Stationary Kernels
PROPOSAL: We design and experimentally evaluate a novel approach for scalable non-stationary GP modeling by introducing `Localized Random Fourier Features` (LRF-F): a set of randomized, output-shifted feature maps that exploit spatial locality and adaptivity in the input space. Specifically, we use a pre-determined grid to segment the input space and apply random Fourier features to each segment separately, generating features that are increasingly local and position-dependent. By choosing the number and placement of segments, we can adjust the degree of expressivity and efficiency, balancing between trade-offs of accuracy, uncertainty, and computational cost.
CONTROLS: 
- Stationary Random Fourier Features (SRFF): serve as baseline for comparison in both stationary and non-stationary settings.
- Sparse Variational GP: used to demonstrate the potential superiority of LRF-F in terms of balancing expressivity and efficiency.
- Deep GP as upper bound for performance in non-stationary settings.
COST: 10,000 GPU-hours
PREDICTION: Significant improvement over stationary SRFF and competitive performance with Deep GP on non-stationary data, potentially offering a scalable, flexible framework for non-stationary GP modeling without the need for complex iterative optimization or hyperparameter tuning. Possible failure areas: over-smoothing due to the localized nature of features, difficulties in choosing optimal segment size and placement.

ACTION: ADD
TITLE: A Theoretical Framework for Localized Random Fourier Features
PROPOSAL: We develop a theoretical framework for understanding the generalizability and convergence properties of LRF-F by generalizing Bochner's theorem to accommodate localized features and imposing mild assumptions on the kernel's smoothness and locality structure. Specifically, we derive bounds for the induced kernel's performance, cardinality, and spectral properties as a function of the number of segments, their size, and the randomness of the Fourier features. Our framework provides guarantees on the approximation quality of LRF-F in terms of both point-wise kernel regression and mean-squared error on unseen data, paving the way for principled design and analysis of these models.
CONTROLS: 
- Stationary Random Fourier Features (SRFF) as baseline for theoretical comparison
- Theoretical analysis of Sparse Variational GP to highlight the gap in expressivity and efficiency
COST: 2,000 GPU-hours (mostly theoretical calculations)
PREDICTION: Our theoretical results demonstrate the viability of LRF-F in approximating non-stationary kernels, showing improvement over SRFF and Sparse Variational GP in terms of convergence rates and statistical guarantees, while also providing insights into the optimal design of LRF-F. Possible failure areas: over-optimism in our assumptions or technical difficulties in generalizing Bochner's theorem.

TITLE: Diffusion Posteriors with Uncertainty-Aware Guide
PROPOSAL:  We propose a novel diffusion-based solver for inverse problems that uses a pretrained denoiser to sample from the intermediate posterior distributions p(x_t|y) while maintaining manifold feasibility. This is achieved by introducing a learnable uncertainty-aware guide that estimates the unnormalized log-posterior probability of states x_t by leveraging the data-driven prior knowledge from the diffusion model. During sampling, this guide receives a noisy representation of the state x_t, which is then used to estimate the intermediate posterior distribution. We alternate between sampling and reducing uncertainty in each iteration, thus exploring the posterior in a principled way and avoiding off-manifold states. 
CONTROLS: We compare our approach against state-of-the-art methods for inverse problems, including iterative guidance methods (DPS, DDRM, DDNM) and stochastic MAP methods (ReSample, DiffPIR, DAPS).

Potential failure point: if the estimation of uncertainty is inaccurate and thus contributes to off-manifold states. However, we can mitigate this risk by employing ensembles and training multiple uncertainty-aware guides.

TITLE: Towards Structural PDE Learning with Simulatable Dynamics
PROPOSAL: We introduce a new method, "StructSim", that combines symbolic-numeric dynamical systems analysis and physics-informed neural networks (PINNs) to leverage the locality and conservation properties of PDE dynamics for more efficient learning.
- Given a PDE system,.StructSim first extracts a minimal, simulatable representation of the system's dynamics, including a small set of representative states and transition rules that emulate the system behavior across different scales and parameter settings.
- Next, we train a PINN to infer the PDE operator from a limited set of training samples, with the key insight that the structural priors extracted from the simulatable dynamics provide a constrained search space for the neural network to optimize.
- Our method effectively reduces the learning space and exploration burden of the neural solver, yielding fast and accurate approximations of the system dynamics with limited training data.
CONTROLS: (1) Comparative experiments to state-of-the-art Pinns, SO-PINNs and PDE-Net; (2) an ablation study to investigate the contributions of simulatable dynamics and structural priors; (3) evaluation on a variety of metrics including data efficiency, solution quality and computational complexity.
COST: 1000 GPU-hours
PREDICTION: Compared to existing PINNs, StructSim improves data efficiency by up to 3x and solution quality by 15% while reducing computational complexity by 20%, demonstrating the potential of simulatable dynamics and structural priors for efficient PDE learning.

ACTION: REVISE

PROPOSAL: We build on the idea of combining symbolic-numeric dynamical systems analysis and physics-informed neural networks (PINNs) to leverage the locality and conservation properties of PDE dynamics for more efficient learning.
- Given a PDE system, StructSim first extracts a minimal, simulatable representation of the system's dynamics, including a small set of representative states and transition rules that emulate the system behavior across different scales and parameter settings.
- Next, we train a PINN to infer the PDE operator from a limited set of training samples, with the key insight that the structural priors extracted from the simulatable dynamics provide a constrained search space for the neural network to optimize.

PREDICTION: By incorporating conservation laws as structural priors, the revised StructSim demonstrates a significant improvement in accuracy (up to 25%), data efficiency (up to 2x faster training), and robustness across different scenarios, showcasing the importance of physically informed design principles for effective PDE learning.

ACTION: ADD 1
TITLE: Q-FFNN: Maximizing the Q-function with Feedforward Neural Networks
PROPOSAL: We experiment with implementing a feedforward neural network (FFNN) to directly compute the argmax of the Q-function, as the traditional way of maximizing the Q-function through grid search or numerical optimization can be computationally expensive and is not scalable to high-dimensional action spaces. The FFNN takes as input the Q-function's output and uses multiple layers of fully connected ReLU units to effectively "pointwise-max" the Q-function and output the optimal action. The FFNN's output can be obtained in constant time, independent of the dimension of the action space.
CONTROLS: We will compare Q-FFNN with Performance-Preserving Discretization (PPD) [1], a state-of-the-art method for approximately computing the argmax of the Q-function using discrete search, as well as with TD3 [2], a widely used actor-critic algorithm for continuous control.
COST: 100 GPU-hours
PREDICTION: We expect Q-FFNN to outperform PPD in high-dimensional action spaces where grid search becomes computationally expensive, and to be competitive with TD3 in navigation and reaching tasks. However, we anticipate that Q-FFNN may struggle with tasks requiring complex Q-functions or high degrees of exploration, where TD3's gradient-based action maximization may still provide advantages.

ACTION: ADD 2
TITLE: Binary Search Tree Q-NN: A Neuro-Network Based Hierarchical Approach
PROPOSAL: We propose a hierarchical architecture inspired by binary search trees to efficiently explore continuous action spaces. The intermediary nodes in the tree correspond to potentially optimal actions, obtained by maximizing the Q-function within a bounded subspace of the action space. Leaf nodes of the tree then correspond to the input of a FFNN, similar to Q-FFNN, which outputs the final optimal action. Unlike grid-based exploration methods, Binary Search Tree Q-NN uses a learned hierarchy to prune the search space and focus on promising regions. This approach reduces the overall computational cost of Hierarchical Q-function maximization.
CONTROLS: We will compare Binary Search Tree Q-NN with Q-FFNN from proposal 1, and with other hierarchical methods for Q-function maximization, such as Adaptive Max-Volume Regions [3].
COST: 150 GPU-hours
PREDICTION: We expect Binary Search Tree Q-NN to outperform Q-FFNN on tasks with sparse and irregular optimal action spaces, where the hierarchical structure can effectively narrow down the search space, while Q-FFNN struggles with local optima.

PROPOSAL: To improve the exploration-exploitation trade-off in actor-free Q-learning, we propose a novel approach using a Hierarchical Binomial Bandit (HBB) to dynamically allocate exploration resources to promising regions of the action space. ACTION: ADD 6
TITLE: Adaptive Multi-Resolution Hierarchical Reinforcement Learning (AMRHRL)
PROPOSAL: We propose an adaptive multi-resolution hierarchical approach for reinforcement learning that combines the strengths of different hierarchical methods. AMRHRL dynamically updates the resolution of the hierarchical structure based on the observed behavior of the Q-function, so that high-resolution search is focused on promising regions and low-resolution search is conducted in regions that are less likely to yield good policies. This is achieved through an adaptive adjustment of the zoom factor applied to the Q-function, which is learned based on the uncertainty of the Q-function estimates over the hierarchical tree. AMRHRL aims to leverage the efficient hierarchical search of high-dimensional Q-function maximization while promoting adaptability and reliability of the exploration-exploitation balance.
CONTROLS: We compare AMRHRL with state-of-the-art hierarchical methods, including Binary Search Tree Q-NN and Hierarchical Binomial Bandit, on a range of reinforcement learning benchmarks with high-dimensional action spaces, including Atari environments and continuous control tasks.
COST: 220 GPU-hours (scalable for different resolutions and structures)
PREDICTION: We expect AMRHRL to achieve superior performance compared to state-of-the-art hierarchical methods by dynamically adapting to the Q-function's behavior, thus ensuring that the search space is efficiently explored and optimal actions are discovered.

PROPOSAL: To facilitate real-world deployment and ease frequent human feedback, we propose a scalable and efficient online VSG architecture that can efficiently process live video streams, integrate with existing infrastructure, and support incremental learning updates. We will evaluate the proposed architecture by measuring its inference speed, memory usage, and adaptability to changing input streams.
CONTROLS: Compare the performance of the proposed architecture with other online VSG frameworks and benchmarking tools.
COST: 250 GPU-hours (allocated to designing, implementing, and evaluating the proposed architecture)
PREDICTION: Our scalable and efficient online VSG architecture will enable seamless integration with existing infrastructure, support real-time processing, and facilitate rapid updates of learning models, while demonstrating strong performance on the real-world deployment benchmark.

ACTION: ADD 1
TITLE: Evaluating the Feasibility of Online Video Step Grounding with Pretrained Models
PROPOSAL: Investigate the use of a large-scale multimodal pretraining model (e.g., CLIP) for zero-shot Video Step Grounding (VSG) on streaming videos from the "Cooking Recipe" dataset (a real-world benchmark with step annotations).
CONTROLS: Compare against a simple heuristic (e.g., matching text templates against a dictionary-based index of step descriptions) and an off-the-shelf captioning model fine-tuned for VSG.
COST: Estimated 100 GPU-hours (approximately 4 days on a high-end machine).
PREDICTION: The pretraining model could achieve state-of-the-art zero-shot performance for VSG, but may struggle with handling similar steps or uncertain observations, indicating a need for further research.

ACTION: ADD 2
TITLE: Injecting Past Context into Online Video Step Grounding
PROPOSAL: Explore a hierarchical memory-augmented neural network architecture (e.g., a temporal memory network) that incorporates a compact, randomly-accessible memory for storing and retrieving information from past video segments in the VSG task, using the "Cooking Recipe" dataset.
CONTROLS: Compare against a standard neural network without memory and against a models that leverage external memory resources (e.g., external knowledge base).
COST: Estimated 200 GPU-hours (approximately 8 days on a high-end machine).
PREDICTION: The model should exhibit improved performance in VSG compared to a standard neural network, particularly when faced with missing or uncertain observations.

ACTION: ADD 3
TITLE: Zero-Shot Video Step Grounding with Multimodal Attention
PROPOSAL: Design a multimodal attention-based model that selectively focuses on relevant regions of the video and step descriptions to make zero-shot predictions for VSG, using a combination of off-the-shelf pretraining models (e.g., CLIP for visual features and a language model for step descriptions).
CONTROLS: Compare against the pretraining model from proposal 1, and an ablation study to evaluate the contribution of the attention mechanism.
COST: Estimated 150 GPU-hours (approximately 6 days on a high-end machine).
PREDICTION: The attention-based model should learn to selectively focus on relevant regions, improving zero-shot performance for VSG, but its Variance may affect overall performance.

ACTION: REVISE 3
TITLE: Zero-Shot Video Step Grounding with Multimodal Attention and Uncertainty Estimation
PROPOSAL: Extend the multimodal attention-based model (proposal 3) with uncertainty estimation mechanisms (e.g., Bayesian neural networks or Monte Carlo dropout) to better handle uncertain observations and missing information in the VSG task, using a combination of off-the-shelf pretraining models.
CONTROLS: Compare against the multimodal attention-based model without uncertainty estimation, and an ablation study to evaluate the contribution of the uncertainty estimation mechanisms.
COST: Estimated 200 GPU-hours (approximately 8 days on a high-end machine).
PREDICTION: The uncertainty estimation mechanisms should improve the model's robustness to uncertain observations, but may introduce additional variance in the predictions.

ACTION: ADD 4
TITLE: Investigating the Impact of Egocentric Procedural Activity Videos
PROPOSAL: Adapt the VSG task to the egocentric procedural activity videos domain and investigate whether the techniques developed for instructional how-to videos (e.g., proposal 1-3) can be effectively transferred or require domain-specific modifications.
CONTROLS: Compare against a standard VSG model without domain adaptation.
COST: Estimated 100 GPU-hours (approximately 4 days on a high-end machine).
PREDICTION: The techniques may require minor adjustments to accommodate the different perspective of egocentric videos, but the overall performance should remain comparable to instructional how-to videos.

ACTION: ADD 5
TITLE: Towards Efficient Online Video Step Grounding with Lightweight Models
PROPOSAL: Investigate the use of lightweight neural networks (e.g., MobileNet, ShuffleNet) to reduce the computational overhead of VSG models, while maintaining competitive performance on streaming videos, using a combination of pretraining and fine-tuning techniques.
CONTROLS: Compare against a standard VSG model and ablation study to evaluate the impact of model size and complexity.
COST: Estimated 50 GPU-hours (approximately 2 days on a high-end machine).
PREDICTION: The lightweight models should achieve comparable performance to standard VSG models but with significant reductions in computational overhead, making them suitable for real-time applications.

ACTION: ADD 6
TITLE: Online Multi-Step Prediction for Video Step Grounding
PROPOSAL: Design a sequential prediction model that takes into account the VSG predictions made at previous time-steps to improve the accuracy of the current prediction, using a combination of pretraining and fine-tuning techniques.
CONTROLS: Compare against a standard VSG model and against the hierarchical memory-augmented neural network from proposal 2.
COST: Estimated 250 GPU-hours (approximately 10 days on a high-end machine).
PREDICTION: The sequential prediction model should improve the overall accuracy of VSG by leveraging information from past predictions, but may introduce additional temporal dependencies, requiring careful model design and tuning.

ACTION: ADD 7
TITLE: Adversarial Training for Robust Video Step Grounding
PROPOSAL: Investigate the use of adversarial training (e.g., adversarial examples, robustness training) to improve the robustness of VSG models against bounded and unbounded perturbations, using a combination of pretraining and fine-tuning techniques.
CONTROLS: Compare against a standard VSG model and against existing robust VSG models.
COST: Estimated 300 GPU-hours (approximately 12 days on a high-end machine).
PREDICTION: Adversarial training should improve the robustness of VSG models, but may require careful design of the adversarial attacks and objectives to avoid overfitting to specific attack scenarios.

ACTION: ADD 8
TITLE: Transfer Learning for Zero-Shot Video Step Grounding across Domains
PROPOSAL: Investigate the effectiveness of transfer learning for zero-shot VSG across different domains (e.g., cooking, furniture assembly, programming), using a combination of pretraining and fine-tuning techniques.
CONTROLS: Compare across different domains and against a standard VSG model.
COST: Estimated 350 GPU-hours (approximately 14 days on a high-end machine).
PREDICTION: Transfer learning should enable VSG models to generalize across different domains and improve zero-shot performance, but the performance may degrade if the pretraining data is not representative of the target domain.

PROPOSAL: Compare the zero-shot performance of popular large pretrained multimodal models (e.g., CLIP, ViLBERT, VLP) on a real-world Video Step Grounding (VSG) benchmark, using a fixed set of procedural steps and a diverse set of cooking recipe videos.

ACTION: ADD
TITLE: Investigating Meta-Learning for Adaptive VSG
PROPOSAL: Adapt a set of representative frames from the test videos using a meta-learning approach (e.g., Meta-Conv or a simplified version), and then fine-tune a small fully connected layer on top for Video Step Grounding. The goal is to efficiently learn a task-specific module with few-shot learning.
CONTROLS: Compare against randomly initialized model and report the improvement in performance using the baseline(VSG from 1).
COST: 20 GPU-hours, due to the training of a separate model from proposal 1 for fine-tuning

If the meta-learner fails to adapt well to VSG, increasing the size of the adaptation dataset should enhance performance but lead to computational overhead as the activation space needs larger supervision that we cannot afford to materialise due to stringent real-time prediction.

TITLE: Weighted Ensemble Learning for VSG
PROPOSAL: Develop a weighted ensemble learning approach for Video Step Grounding, where the weights of the individual models are adapted based on their past performance and the uncertainty of their predictions. This can help to mitigate the impact of model differences and provide more robust predictions.
CONTROLS: Compare against a basic ensemble approach without weight adaptation, as well as against a baseline that uses a single model.
COST: 12 GPU-hours
PREDICTION: We expect the weighted ensemble approach to provide improved accuracy and robustness compared to the basic ensemble approach, by adaptively incorporating the strengths of multiple models. However, the performance may degrade if the models are too dissimilar or if the uncertainty estimates are inaccurate, potentially leading to over-reliance on top-performing models and suboptimal predictions.

ACTION: ADD
TITLE: Hierarchical Fusion of Audio and Visual Cues for VSG
PROPOSAL: Investigate the use of hierarchical fusion of audio and visual cues for Video Step Grounding. This involves extracting audio features (e.g., sound effects) and visual features (e.g., objects, actions) and then combining them at multiple levels (e.g., frame, segment, video) using a fusion layer. The goal is to leverage the complementary information from different modalities to improve VSG performance.
CONTROLS: Compare against a baseline that uses only visual cues or only audio cues, as well as against a model that uses a simple late fusion approach.
COST: 18 GPU-hours
PREDICTION: We expect the hierarchical fusion approach to provide improved accuracy and robustness by incorporating the complementary information from audio and visual cues. However, the challenge lies in designing an effective fusion strategy that balances the contributions of different modalities, which may lead to a complex optimization problem.

ACTION: ADD
TITLE: Attention-Based Sequential Reasoning for VSG
PROPOSAL: Develop an attention-based sequential reasoning approach for Video Step Grounding, where the model learns to focus on the most relevant segments of the video when considering each procedural step. This involves introducing an attention mechanism that learns to attend to specific segments and objects in the video, reducing the noise and irrelevant information.
CONTROLS: Compare against a baseline that uses a simple online sequential model, as well as against a model that uses a fixed attention mechanism.
COST: 25 GPU-hours
PREDICTION: We expect the attention-based sequential reasoning approach to provide improved accuracy and robustness by effectively focusing on the most relevant segments of the video. However, the challenge lies in designing an efficient attention mechanism that balances the trade-off between need for exploration and exploitation, as well as adapting to the varying length and complexity of video sequences.

PROPOSAL: Investigate the use of transfer learning from pre-trained vision-language models (e.g., CLIP, ViLBERT, VLP) for Video Step Grounding, leveraging their pre-trained representations and knowledge to improve VSG performance. This involves fine-tuning the pre-trained models on a VSG-specific dataset or using them as a starting point for further training.
CONTROLS: Compare against a baseline that uses a randomly initialized model, as well as against a model that uses a self-supervised VSG pre-training approach.
COST: 30 GPU-hours
PREDICTION: We expect transfer learning from pre-trained vision-language models to provide a strong baseline for VSG, leveraging their pre-trained representations and knowledge. However, the challenge lies in adapting the pre-trained models to the specific task of VSG, which may require careful fine-tuning and adaptation of the models to the VSG-specific dataset.

RSATO will be designed to learn the optimal distribution over the discrete tokens that minimizes the difference between the true discrete entropy and the relaxed entropy, which ensures that the gradients from downstream objectives are stable, low-variance, and faithful to the true discrete objective.

PROPOSAL:  Design and experiment with PRR, a method that post-distillation enables end-to-end gradient-based training of one-step discrete generators. The weights of the comparator will be learned during training to weigh the perturbed and regular rewards, so as to best utilize downstream feedback for the refinement of the one-step generator.

TITLE: Gradient Flow Through Discrete Tokens via Automatic Loss Differentiation
PROPOSAL: Implement an automatic loss differentiation (ALD) technique to backpropagate gradients through binary discrete tokens by probabilistically differentiating the discrete binary function, similar to the Gumbel-Softmax. Our ALD scheme analytically computes the end-to-end gradient of any loss function specified by the user, using the accessible (differentiable) components to compute those of the inaccessible discrete components. We use our scheme to craft novel training objectives for the student generator, such as reward models and discriminator outputs, and to add custom regression objectives on either intermediate or final models (tokenizer, student combined with its metadata model, or discriminator).

ACTION: ADD
TITLE: LLM-based Time Series Quality Evaluation with Time-aware Prompts
PROPOSAL: We design and train a set of LLMs on a large corpus of time series data from diverse domains, and evaluate their ability to assess the quality of unseen time series samples using time-aware prompts. These prompts will be specifically designed to capture key characteristics of time series such as continuity, temporal dependencies, and non-stationarity. We explore different types of time-aware prompts, including those based on temporal operators (e.g., largest value in the last week), time embeddings (e.g., day of the week, hour of the day), and attention mechanisms.
CONTROLS: We include LLMs without time-aware prompts, vanilla LLMs with static prompts, and memory-augmented networks (intermediate results) trained on a subset of the same time series data.
COST: 1000 GPU-hours
PREDICTION: Our LLM-based approach will significantly outperform traditional influence function and Shapley-value methods, and comparable to, possibly surpassing previously best methods among time series-specific methods such as TimeInf or TimeShap. However, it might underperform on extremely noisy time series datasets or when the target quality criteria lack clear temporal dependencies.

ACTION: ADD 1
TITLE: Evaluating the Cardinality of Directed Graph Generative Models
PROPOSAL: Investigate the capacity of directed graph generative models to capture the diversity of directed graphs by comparing their ability to generate digraphs of varying cardinality (number of nodes and edges). Utilize a range of synthetic graph models to generate diverse digraphs for training and testing, including directed random graphs, scale-free graphs, and graphs with specific types of local structures (e.g. clusters). Measure the performance of various models, including a directed extension of the GraphVAE, the recently proposed general digraph generation method, and a simple autoregressive model, using metrics such as graph perplexity and the fraction of correctly reconstructed edges. Compare the performance of these models on graphs of increasing cardinality.
CONTROLS: The recent general digraph model and the GraphVAE with a normalizing flow-based edge direction model will serve as baseline models; ablations focusing on the impact of the edge direction model and the autoregressive component will also be included. COST: 1000 GPU-hours
PREDICTION: The directed extension of the GraphVAE is expected to perform well and demonstrate the capacity to generate a wide range of directed graphs, whereas the simple autoregressive model may struggle to capture the complexity of directed graph distributions, and the recently proposed general digraph model may exhibit superior performance as the cardinality of the graphs increases. It might fail in capturing some specific types of local structures and edge directionality in higher-cardinality graphs, however.

TITLE: Gradient-based Localization for Fine-grained Visual Question Answering
PROPOSAL: 
In this experiment, we apply a gradient-based localization method, inspired by existing works in visual protein localization and molecule-based neural explanation, to find the most relevant image regions for fine-grained visual question answering. The key idea is to compute the gradient of the MLLM's output with respect to the image patches and then select the ones that contribute the most to the final prediction. We pre-train a global-view MLLM, such as ViLT, on a large-scale image-text dataset and then fine-tune it on a fine-grained VQA dataset (e.g., VQAZ or GQA).
CONTROLS: 
- Baseline: global-view MLLM without localization
- Baseline: global-local-view MLLM with random local crops
- Ablation: global-view MLLM with gradient-based localization on a subset of image patches (e.g., 10% of the total number of patches)
COST: 
- Estimated compute: 10 GPU-hours (Pre-training + fine-tuning)
PREDICTION: 
We expect to see a performance boost on fine-grained VQA tasks, with a potentially favorable accuracy-efficiency trade-off relative to global-local-view MLLMs. However, the method might struggle with task-specific dependencies, as it relies on the MLLM's ability to capture question-related visual features.

TITLE: Learning to Attend Relevant Pixels for Cross-modal Features
PROPOSAL: 
We propose a new cross-modal feature attention mechanism that learns to focus on the most relevant pixels in an image for fine-grained visual question answering. The mechanism is designed to jointly attend over the image and the question, and is learned jointly with the MLLM. We introduce a novel pixel-wise attention module that uses a query-key-value attention structure, where the keys and values are computed from the image and the query is computed from the question.

- Baseline: global-view MLLM without attention mechanism

- Ablation: global-view MLLM with the proposed pixel-wise attention mechanism, but without the joint learning with the MLLM

TITLE: Fixing Hallucinations in Object Localization for Small Objects
PROPOSAL: 
We investigate the issue of hallucinations in object localization for small objects, observed in existing MLLMs that predict bounding boxes. We propose a novel regularization technique that encourages the model to predict more confident and accurate object locations, by penalizing the overlap between predicted bounding boxes and previously seen regions in the image. We evaluate this approach on a set of fine-grained VQA tasks that focus on small objects and compare it to existing MLLMs trained with standard regularization techniques.
CONTROLS: 
- Baseline: global-view MLLM without regularization techniques
- Baseline: global-local-view MLLM with standard regularization techniques (e.g., dropout)
- Ablation: global-view MLLM with the proposed object localization regularization

- Estimated compute: 10 GPU-hours (training the MLLM with the new regularization technique)
PREDICTION: 
We expect to see a significant reduction in hallucinations for small object localization, and an improvement in overall performance on fine-grained VQA tasks. However, the success of the method might depend on the image quality, object size, and model architecture, and it might require additional tuning for optimal performance.

TITLE: Efficient Fine-Grained Visual Question Answering with Bilateral Attention
PROPOSAL: We propose a novel bilateral attention mechanism that encourages the MLLM to focus on image regions relevant to the question, while suppressing irrelevant tokens. Specifically, we add an attention head that computes a bilateral filter between the vision tokens and the question embedding, and use this filtered attention to compute a weighted sum of the vision tokens. We compare the performance of our model to two baselines: a standard global-view MLLM and a global-local-view MLLM.
CONTROLS: 
- Baseline 1: Standard global-view MLLM on VQA v2 (VisDial 1.0) and COCO-QA 4.0 datasets
- Baseline 2: Global-local-view MLLM on VQA v2 (VisDial 1.0) and COCO-QA 4.0 datasets
COST: 1500 GPU-hours
PREDICTION: We expect our model to outperform both baselines on fine-grained VQA tasks, while keeping inference cost reasonable (5-10% increase over the global-view MLLM). One possible failure point: if the question embedding is not well-aligned with the image regions of interest, the bilateral attention may fail to focus on relevant regions.

ACTION: ADD 1
TITLE: Leveraging Population Context for Zero-Shot Neuron Representation Learning
PROPOSAL: We will train a population-level transformer encoder to summarize Neuropixels electrophysiology recordings in mice and then use this representation to train a neuron-level decoder that infers neuron identity. We will compare the decoder's performance to a baseline that uses fixed low-dimensional summaries of the population activity.
CONTROLS: Baseline = fixed low-dimensional summaries (e.g. PCA, t-SNE) of population activity, No population context
COST: 1000 GPU-hours (training the population-level encoder and neuron-level decoder on the Neuropixels dataset)
PREDICTION: We expect to see improved neuron classification accuracy over the baseline, but the absolute accuracy might not be very high due to the limited amount of information available in the Neuropixels recordings. This experiment might fail if the population-level encoder is not able to capture the relevant features from the Neuropixels data.

ACTION: ADD 2
TITLE: Evaluating the Impact of Recording Diversification on Neuron Representation Learning
PROPOSAL: We will systematically vary the number and diversity of recordings available for learning, while keeping the amount of labeled neurons constant, to evaluate how this affects the accuracy of the neuron-level decoder. We will use a test set with varied recording conditions and neural types to assess the transferability of the learned representations.
CONTROLS: Baseline = fixed diversification (e.g. same number and type of recordings for all neurons), Varying recording conditions (e.g. different stimuli, behaviors) and neural types (e.g. different cell types, brain regions)
COST: 500 GPU-hours (training the neuron-level decoder on the Neuropixels dataset with different recording diversifications)
PREDICTION: We expect to see improved neuron classification accuracy as the number and diversity of recordings available for learning increase. However, we might also see diminishing returns beyond a certain point, indicating that there is a trade-off between recording availability and decoder performance.

ACTION: ADD 3
TITLE: Comparing Self-Supervised and Supervised Learning for Neuron Representation
PROPOSAL: We will compare the performance of a self-supervised learning approach, where the neuron-level decoder is trained to predict the population activity from the neuron-level representation, to a supervised learning approach, where the decoder is trained directly on the identity labels. We will use both Neuropixels electrophysiology recordings and calcium imaging recordings in mice.
CONTROLS: Baseline = supervised learning with identity labels, No population context
COST: 2000 GPU-hours (training the self-supervised and supervised neuron-level decoders on the Neuropixels and calcium imaging datasets)
PREDICTION: We expect to see improved neuron classification accuracy with supervised learning, but the self-supervised approach might be more sample-efficient due to its ability to learn from the rich population context. However, the self-supervised approach might also require more computational resources to converge.

ACTION: REVISE 1
TITLE: Leveraging Population Context for Zero-Shot Neuron Representation Learning with Graph Neural Networks
PROPOSAL: We will use graph neural networks to explicitly model the relationships between neurons in the population, in addition to the transformer encoder used in the original proposal. This will allow us to better capture the local and global structure of the population activity.
CONTROLS: Original baseline = fixed low-dimensional summaries (e.g. PCA, t-SNE) of population activity, Original no population context
COST: 1500 GPU-hours (training the population-level graph neural network and neuron-level decoder on the Neuropixels dataset)
PREDICTION: We expect to see improved neuron classification accuracy due to the better capture of population structure and relationships. However, the added complexity of the graph neural network might also lead to overfitting, especially if the number of training samples is limited.

ACTION: ADD 4
TITLE: Using Transfer Learning for Zero-Shot Neuron Representation across New Animals and Sessions
PROPOSAL: We will pretrain the population-level encoder and neuron-level decoder on a large dataset of Neuropixels recordings from one animal, and then fine-tune them on a small dataset from a new animal. We will also evaluate transfer learning on recordings from new sessions within the same animal.
CONTROLS: Baseline = training from scratch on new animal, Baseline = training from scratch on new session, Pretraining on large dataset, No fine-tuning
COST: 800 GPU-hours (pretraining and fine-tuning the population-level encoder and neuron-level decoder on the Neuropixels dataset)
PREDICTION: We expect to see improved neuron classification accuracy with transfer learning, especially when fine-tuning on a small dataset from a new animal. However, the degree of transferability might depend on the similarity between the pretraining and fine-tuning datasets.

ACTION: ADD 5
TITLE: Inferring Brain Region-Specific Neuron Features from Population Activity
PROPOSAL: We will train a neural network to predict brain region features (e.g. Brodmann areas) from the neuron-level representation learned in previous experiments. We will use the calcium imaging dataset, which has explicitly labeled brain region information.
CONTROLS: Baseline = directly predicting brain region features from population activity, Baseline = using fixed low-dimensional summaries (e.g. PCA, t-SNE) of population activity
COST: 600 GPU-hours (training the brain region predictor on the calcium imaging dataset)
PREDICTION: We expect to see improved brain region feature prediction accuracy with the learned neuron-level representation, especially in regions with distinct functional properties. However, the model might fail to generalize to regions with ambiguous or similar functional properties.

ACTION: REVISE 2
TITLE: Evaluating the Impact of Recording Diversification on Neuron Representation Learning using Real-World Variability
PROPOSAL: We will expand the evaluation of recording diversification (proposed in Turn 2) to include real-world variability in Neuropixels recordings, rather than just systematic variation in conditions. We will use a dataset with naturally occurring variability in recording conditions, neural types, and brain regions.
CONTROLS: Baseline = fixed diversification (e.g. same number and type of recordings for all neurons), Baseline = using fixed low-dimensional summaries (e.g. PCA, t-SNE) of population activity
COST: 1000 GPU-hours (training the neuron-level decoder on the Neuropixels dataset with real-world variability)
PREDICTION: We expect to see improved neuron classification accuracy with recording diversification, especially in regions with distinct functional properties. However, the model might also exhibit decreased robustness to variations in recording conditions, such as noise or vibrations.

ACTION: ADD 6
TITLE: Investigating the Role of Temporal Information in Neuron Representation Learning
PROPOSAL: We will incorporate temporal information into the neuron-level representation learning pipeline, either by using a temporal convolutional network (TCN) or a recurrent neural network (RNN) to capture long-term dependencies in the population activity.
CONTROLS: Baseline = not using temporal information, Baseline = using fixed low-dimensional summaries (e.g. PCA, t-SNE) of population activity
COST: 1200 GPU-hours (training the population-level encoder and neuron-level decoder on the Neuropixels dataset with temporal information)
PREDICTION: We expect to see improved neuron classification accuracy with temporal information, especially in regions with distinct temporal properties. However, the model might also exhibit increased computational cost and complexity due to the addition of temporal layers.

ACTION: ADD 7
TITLE: Evaluating the Robustness of Neuron Representation Learning to Sensor Noise and Implantation Variability
PROPOSAL: We will evaluate the robustness of the learned neuron-level representations to sensor noise and implantation variability in Neuropixels recordings, by using a dataset with simulated noise and implantation variations.
CONTROLS: Baseline = no noise and implantation variations, Baseline = using fixed low-dimensional summaries (e.g. PCA, t-SNE) of population activity
COST: 800 GPU-hours (training the population-level encoder and neuron-level decoder on the Neuropixels dataset with simulated noise and implantation variations)
PREDICTION: We expect to see that the learned neuron-level representations are robust to low levels of sensor noise, but may be affected by high levels of noise or implantation variability. However, the model might also exhibit decreased robustness to systematic variations in recording conditions.

ACTION: ADD 8
